title: Why do people find sequels, reboots, remakes or prequels inherently problematic?

commenti.body: There's nothing *inherently* wrong with sequels, prequels, remakes and reboots. They *can* all be done well. The problem is that big corporations love them too much since they come with a built-in audience, so they often become lazy, political, or nothing more than nostalgia-bait. When they prioritise nostalgia over story, you end up with drivel.

I think it's just a question of quality. 

Godfather 2 was great, all the mission impossible movies after 2/3 are great, and you could both call them a reboot and sequels as the movies change tone quite a bit from mission impossible 1.

Terminator 2 was probably the best terminator. 

But a lot of times a movie is made and it is held in high regard and at the time of filming no one was considering it s franchise vehicle so they don't set up future movies quite the way they usually need to be set up, especially movies based on books that were stand alone. 

One could argue that studio meddling plays a factor in poorly received sequels or prequels, and often times either the creators of the original movie as well as the actors aren't involved at all with the subsequent movies. 

But if you look at a movie like furiousa and fury road which were made by the same guy that made mad max and road warrior and they are a serious passion project from the original creator they turn out great. 

So sequels and prequels can work but they need ideal conditions to succeed where everyone actually enjoys it. 

I think sequels in general are getting better, there are just so many of them that it's easy to look at them, at least most of them, as unnecessary. If you make a sequel and it doesn't have the same tone, feel, or innovation of an original movie that people love, it's going to fail.

I don’t think the problem is that they’re “inherently” problematic or uncreative, I think there are plenty of examples where the opposite is true.

I think it’s just that it’s clear even to laymen that Hollywood has found them to be their best chance at return on investment right now, and it’s become an over saturation problem above anything else. There’s this feeling that cinema market is overloaded with repackaged movies that feels like they were pitched by execs from the same four monopolies and not creatives.

How many good prequels can you name? 

Good sequels happen a bit more often, but usually when part of a pre-planned series/franchise. For every Aliens and Terminator 2, you get a dozen Jaws 2. 

Even when you do get a Terminator 2, look at the rest of the franchise and how rubbish it’s been. 

It’s the same with reboots and remakes. Invisible Man from 2019 was awesome. But then you get the Old Boy remake, Ghostbusters reboot, Pyscho remake, etc.

There have been very very very few successful reboots/remakes. Almost all the successful ones have been from mega huge properties that already had fan bases. Batman, Star Trek, Bond. 

Then sometimes you get a Creed, 21 Jump Street, Mad Max, Ocean’s 11.

I wouldn't use the word problematic... like ever, I hate that word. That said, there's nothing inherently wrong with sequels and franchises and reboots. But in moving away from original material it does kind of put creatives on the back foot.


There used to be a market for original spec scripts. Someone could write an original script and if it were good or marketable and it ended up in the right hands, a screenwriting would get paid for it, meaning she was able to pay the bills and go to work on the next script. These days, you can't just write a Marvel movie. Marvel owns the IP. 


The way in for a writer is to get hired by Marvel and work your ways into the writers room. So now, writers have to go through the same credentialing process as bankers and lawyers and consultants, which means they're going to be a more homogeneous group and be overall more risk-averse. I don't think that's good for art.

Thirty years ago, when people heard “sequel”, they could almost rightly assume it would be crap. Godfather Pt 2 was the exception, and that’s because it partially adapted sections of the original novel and retained the involvement of the original author, Mario Puzo, in envisioning the sequel.

Of course there's nothing inherently wrong with them. Some of the best films ever are sequels, remakes, etc. It's the overreliance on them, and the "safe" approach to marketing that generates them, and yes, the shit quality of many of them. And everything comes with tradeoffs. There's only so much capital in the film industry with which to produce films. For every sequel or reboot that gets made, some number of original projects don't. Which is lamentable.

For me it's definitely the latter, I used to have an open mind. The Ghostbuster remake from 2016 is fine. It can't touch the original but I like that they tried something original. Then you have Ghostbuster Afterlife, which is one of the worst films I have ever seen. The same is true for the Jurassic World series, the first one is still watchable, it's the first time we see a functioning park and we have an original Dinosaur and well the plot is incredibly stupid but we get some nice action and some kills. Fallen Kingdom and Dominion are such complete failures on every level that I can't even get into detail.

"Keep the lights on for the industry" is a terrible phrase to justify the inflated salaries of all the already overly recognised individuals involved in productions.

"Big name" directors, actors, producers, especially taking huge salaries and profits building fortunes when they could reduce the overall cost of productions, increase production times, increase wages for all the hundreds of other people actually essential to the industry...

Urgh. It drives me mad.

Hollywood is in the business of making money, not making films. They sell products not art, they help enhance the profile of certain leading actors in order to sell future productions and help inflate the branding of certain directors.

So little of it is actually based on talent, merit, ability or craft.

Long about way of answering your question, but it's healthy to have some cynicism around reboots and requels because no one is remaking flawed movies and improving them, they're remaking or adding to existing and recognised brands that made money in order to make money.

Some of the issues come from the fact that you have to somewhat introduce the characters *again* and replace them in a different context. Not only the script has to do that for the new viewers, but it's also a problem because a story is tailored-made for the main character. What he faces is telling on who he is, what he has to overcome. If he has overcome something in a previous movie, it's difficult to put him back at square one after all of his achievements. It's also hard to represent a threat as impactful when it has a previous point of comparison. And when a movie became a classic, I think the audience often sees it as monolithic, something complete by itself. That's the feeling you want to have at the end of a good movie, a sort of closure, even if it means ending up in a complete mystery (then it doesn't want to be resolved) or in failure (then it's a tragedy which is hard to restart).

There aren't those issues with prequels for example. It's easier to look at a hero and search for his previous states, how he became worthy of the source material. I'm pretty sure that's why we see so many back-and-forth between prequels and sequels nowadays, looking back at previous struggles opens up new angles in the future and in the sequels of the origin material too. Once it's been established that there is a progression in multiple steps, it's easier to have our hero face a new obstacles that forces him to evolve again, he's not set in stone as much.

And then... There are those issues multiplied by the number of important secondary characters... If it's true for the hero, it's also true for the romantic interest, the side-kick, the villain, and it can even be applied to their relationships in itself. If you do a prequel or a sequel on multiple characters, you have to make their relationships somewhat different and it "breaks" a sort of illusion we have of a perfectly lasting relationship. When a new character is introduced, it's the same thing. Why wasn't he there before? Is he less important because he is a latter addition? Who does he replace? You get those weird comparisons that you have to take into account. The ideal hero is often someone who can integrates anyone in their lives, but it's also someone who doesn't cling on people and doesn't let them down either. If a script has to do one of those things, then it almost always needs to become the center of the emotional trajectory of the narrative. But then it stills enters in a sort of competition with the other relationships that existed previously. In an original movie, you can easily have a friendship at its own place, separated from a romance, the two don't necessarily threaten each other because they have a sort of respectful balance. When you introduce a new relationship, it undoes the original balance and since there is usually 3 or more emotional centers in a script (which is a very unstable mix), it's hard to land back onto an equilibrium.

So the original movie benefits from a sort of idealization because it's limited and well defined, while all sequels and even some prequels make the original plot become more "dynamic". There is no ideal situation anymore, or at least the effort it takes to achieve a comfortable social circle becomes a lot bigger. And because it's so difficult to write, it happens often that the "strings" that hold a script together become more noticeable in a sequel or a prequel. Usually, art is more enjoyable when we don't realize all the work that was put into it. Artists want to make it look easy to help people forget themselves for a while.

Well, I don't. Humans have always liked telling stories of such length that they became serialized: the Gilgamesh epic is in several parts. The Aeneid is a veritable sequel - o dictu horribile - to the Illiad. Wagner's Ring is in four parts, Geothe's Faust is in two... So I don't see anything inherently artistically inferior about doing more than one film about something.

Having said that, there ARE a number of caveats: One, many (but not all) of the examples I gave are not the classic Hollywood sequel in that they're insoluble parts of a greater whole. That immediately sets apart sequels like those for *Jaws* and *Jurassic Park*, but even something like *The Godfather: Part Two*, because in all those cases the original is entirely self-sufficient as a story, and the sequels are added onto it.

Essentially, we're looking at two different types of film series: *anthologies* and *cycles*. The one is a series if detachable "episodes" or vignettes - Indiana Jones, Star Trek, most of the Bonds all fall into this category - and the other is as I said earlier, one story told in multiple parts: the most obvious example being The Lord of the Rings but to a lesser extent Harry Potter and even Star Wars I-VI can be adduced into this category. Obviously its a sliding scale: Marvel, for example, is somewhere between the two.

Of the two, cycles clearly aspire to the ideal of unity that I've outlined above: in theory, a cycle would only be wholly comprehensible and effective if one watched all its entries in order: one couldn't, in theory, omit any entry not change the order and hope to have a satisfying experience. Since this requires much great forethought in terms of storytelling, this sort of filmmaking is much rarer. Instead, we get a good deal of anthologies and those ARE less artistically accomplished for not meeting this age-old ideal of unity.

In both the cases of cycles and anthologies, there is that undefined but palpable point in which the whole thing just becomes that bit too long in the tooth. I think both Marvel and Star Wars are good examples of series that have blown well past that point, and the whole thing becomes that bit too old hat, predictable and ossified.

Beyond that, there are also a couple of other caveats with long running series: one, is when Hollywood insists on making ANOTHER sequel to an entry that was for all intents and purposes a good resolution: the Star Wars sequel trilogy, Marvel's Phase 4, Indiana Jones 4 and 5 and many other such "legacy" sequels are like that. Indiana Jones is obviously an anthology, but even there an entry like The Last Crusade while not being a culmination in, say, the Return of the Jedi sense, DOES represent a clear point of departure: a farewell to the character. To continue past that point would be the equivalent of sitting in the theatre for a film, having it conclude, wind down and cut to credits...and then restart and continue for another 30 minutes... Prequels don't have that problem but they have several other potential snares: they can demystify, and they're not always satisfying to watch in "narrative" order.

sure. but you do agree that on paper these things are not necessarily wrong right?

There are v few good prequels, but that does not mean there cannot be one. A chance to visit an interesting character's or setting's past. Furiosa just this year is a great prequel imho.

I get your point. But the reason for sequels etc is the potential to tell great stories within a previosuly existing world. There is a whole world of fan fiction out there. What if a pro writer gets inspired to tell a great story in an exiting franchise? That is how Aliens happened. He liked the world of Alien and then pitched his ideas to Fox and came up with the script himself.
this is my question, that why would people assume it would be crap?

I can see your point of view. I wouldn't completely dismiss HW as just making money and not films. Or that they just churn out products. That is an insult to the work of thousands or creatives and artists who have worked on films. The way I see it, the higher the budget goes, the lesser artistic merit a film has. But, an artistic merit is always there 99% of the time.

Sure cynism is fine, especially when the batting average of franchise films is not too strong. But I am asking is that is the idea inherently bad?
good point. it is a question of quality indeed.

Great write up mate. You have raised an important consideration. Basically, the pieces are meant to function for the original film and then adding another film can disturb the dynamics established in previous films. It can definitely come up as a challenge.

But there is a counter to that. Look characters and relationships are still contained within a story. And if a story can be continued, why cannot the characters be evolved from their previous states?

People grow in real life too. Some people continue the previous relationships. Some move on to new ones. So that can be replicated in movies too.

Then there is the aspect of telling a new story with new characters in the same setting. For instance, the upcoming Ballerina. it is a separate story in the John Wick world with little connection to the other characters.

I can see your point for sure. But I feel if there is a story worth telling, then those dynamics can be adjusted accordingly.

great reply mr. Geller. So the idea is not bad inherently. It's just that Hollywood has overused it beyond the limit. It has continued to tell stories in franchises when there was no storytelling purpose to, but perhaps the main motivation was money. 

Is that what you saying?

But if a story is worth telling in an existing film series, whether a prequel or sequel or spinoff then there is nothing wrong with it? As long as it is made with passion and brings something fresh to the series, right? Both the recent Mad Max movies are great examples of this.

I'd go further and say that the idea of reboots/remakes isn't bad either. There are some movies that have not aged too well with time, but do have interesting ideas. Why not revisit them with modern sensibilities and technologies. This ain't a bad idea on paper right?
